persona.bio: Kayla, 27, electrician who owns a one truck business in Phoenix. She is in attics by 7am and on job sites all day; she has no office and works from her Samsung phone in the truck. The paperwork around the job is what drags: writing quotes, sending invoices, texting homeowners about times, chasing payment, asking for reviews. She does quotes on her phone at night, often by talking them through. She tried ChatGPT once to write a review request and forgot about it.

path.role: You’re a self employed electrician with one truck, mostly doing homes in Phoenix.

steps.firstStep: I’m a self employed electrician with one truck, mostly doing home jobs in Phoenix. Each time I finish a site visit, I need a clear written quote for the homeowner. Turn my notes into a clean quote with a parts line, a labor line, a permit fee line, and a total at the bottom. Include a line saying the quote is good for 30 days and a 50% deposit is needed to book. Keep it short, polite and easy to read on a phone. Here are my notes from this visit: [paste your voice memo notes or typed notes here]

steps.note: I’m a self employed electrician with one truck, and most of my work is in homes around Phoenix. I write quotes, invoices and texts to homeowners, so write like a tradesperson talking to a neighbor: plain, friendly and direct. Keep messages short, usually a few sentences. Use simple words and no jargon unless I use it first. Never add details I did not give you, like prices, parts, dates or code rules. If something is missing, put it in square brackets and ask me. Do not make promises for me. I will read everything before it goes out.

steps.title: Your quotes, said out loud, finished as text
steps.read: From now on you say the job out loud and Claude turns it into a finished quote. You already talk it through on a voice memo, so this fits how you work in the truck and at night. Claude writes it in the same layout every time, with parts, labor, permit fee and total, and it only uses what you said.

material.label: Instructions for your assistant
items: I’m a self employed electrician with one truck, doing mostly homes in Phoenix. I’m going to talk through a job after a site visit. Turn what I say into a finished quote I can send to the homeowner. Use this layout: a short line naming the job and the type of home, then parts, labor, permit fee, and the total at the bottom. End with this line: Good for 30 days, 50% deposit to book. Use only the prices, parts and details I say out loud. Never add or guess any. If something is missing, such as a price or a quantity, leave it in square brackets and list what is missing after the quote. Keep the wording plain and friendly, like I’m talking to the homeowner. Give me back the quote as text I can read and send.

material.label: What to say each time
items: The kind of job and the home, for example the type of house and its age.
Each part and how many, with its price.
Labor, and what you charge for it.
The permit fee, if the job needs one.
Anything that is not included, or anything the homeowner needs to do first.
The homeowner’s first name, and how long the quote is good for if it is not 30 days.

steps.title: Your homeowner texts, saved once on your phone
steps.read: Your common homeowner texts now live on your phone’s keyboard. You type a few letters and the full reply is ready to tap in. That keeps your texts consistent while you are on the job site, and you only change a name or a time.

material.label: Your replies
items: Hi [first name], thanks for reaching out. I can come take a look at [address or area] on [day and time]. Does that work for you?
Hi [first name], I’m on my way and should be there around [time]. See you soon.
Hi [first name], your quote is ready. I’ll send it over now. It’s good for 30 days, and a 50% deposit books the job.
Hi [first name], I got your deposit. You’re booked for [day and time]. Let me know if anything changes on your end.
Hi [first name], the work is done and your invoice is on its way. Thanks for choosing me. Call or text if you have any questions.
Hi [first name], a friendly reminder that invoice [number] is still open. Could you let me know when I can expect payment?
Hi [first name], it was good working with you. If you were happy with the job, would you leave me a quick review here? [review link]
Hi [first name], I’m running behind on a job and will be about [amount of time] late. Sorry for the wait, and thanks for your patience.

safeUse: Never type a homeowner’s full name, home address, phone number or gate and door codes into Claude. Use square brackets and add them yourself.
Keep payment details, like card numbers, bank info and account numbers, out of any chat.
Leave out anything that shows when a home is empty or how its security is set up.
Read every quote, invoice and text before it goes out. Check each price, part and total against your own numbers.
Check permit fees and code details against your city’s own sources, not what Claude says.

design.today: You write quotes a few times a week, usually at night after talking the job through on a voice memo. Photos from the site go into your phone, and each quote lists parts, labor, permit fee and a total, good for 30 days with 50% deposit to book.
design.newWay: You keep talking the job through out loud at night, and your assistant turns what you said into a quote in your usual layout: parts, labor, permit fee, total at bottom, 30 day validity and 50% deposit. You read it, fix any number, and send it yourself. It is better for you because the typing and layout are done and you only check the figures.

steps.goal: Get Claude ready on your phone so you can use it from the truck or at night.
Save a short note about you and your business so quotes come out in your voice and your terms.
Make a project for quotes that holds your quote layout and terms in one place.
Set up a saved quote assistant that turns your spoken job notes into a finished quote in your layout.
Pick two or three past quotes, such as the panel upgrade, to use as examples of how you want quotes to look.

material.label: Quote assistant instructions
material.what: Tells the assistant to build a quote with parts, labor, permit fee and total at bottom, using your wording.

material.label: Standard terms
material.what: Holds your 30 day validity and 50% deposit to book, ready to add to every quote.

material.label: Example quote
material.what: Your 200 amp panel upgrade quote kept as a model for layout and tone.

material.label: Missing info prompt
material.what: A short line that makes the assistant ask you about any price or quantity you did not say, instead of guessing.

design.checkPoint: You read the finished quote and check every part, price, permit fee and total against your notes before you send it yourself.

design.today: You text homeowners often, and many of the messages are about the same few things.
design.newWay: Your most common replies are saved on your phone, so a few letters brings up the full message, like arrival times, quote follow ups or a payment reminder. You read each one, adjust the details, and send it. It is better for you because you answer fast from the job site without retyping the same thing.

steps.goal: List the ten things you text homeowners most often, such as running late, confirming a visit and asking for a review.
Get Claude ready on your phone so it can help you word the saved replies.
Have the assistant write a short, friendly version of each of your ten replies in your voice.
Save the ten replies so each one is a few letters away when you text.

material.label: Ten saved replies
material.what: Short texts for your most common homeowner messages, with gaps for name, time or amount.

material.label: Shortcut list
material.what: The few letters that bring up each saved reply, so you can remember them.

material.label: Tone notes
material.what: A few lines on how you sound with homeowners: polite, direct and brief.

design.checkPoint: You read every reply and fill in the name, time or amount before you send it yourself.
